"Jupiter is so big that all the other planets could fit inside it."
"Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to travel all the way to Earth."
"Space is completely silent, because there\'s no air to carry sound."
"Earth takes 365 and a quarter days to orbit the Sun — that\'s why we add a leap day every 4 years."
"The tallest volcano we know of, Olympus Mons on Mars, is about three times taller than Mount Everest."
"Earth is the only planet not named after a Greek or Roman god."
"There are more stars in the universe than grains of sand on all of Earth\'s beaches."
"The Moon drifts about 3.8 cm farther from Earth every year."
"Saturn is so light for its size that it would float in a giant bathtub of water."
"Lightning strikes somewhere on Earth about 100 times every second."
"The Space Station zooms around the whole Earth about once every 90 minutes."
"Auroras glow near the poles when tiny particles from the Sun crash into our air."
"About 70% of Earth\'s surface is covered by ocean."
"Venus is the hottest planet, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun."
"The Great Red Spot on Jupiter is a storm bigger than the whole Earth."
"Earthquakes happen when giant pieces of Earth\'s crust slip past each other."
"The Sun is actually white — our air is what makes it look yellow."
"Comets are giant balls of ice and dust that grow glowing tails near the Sun."
"If you could drive a car straight up, you\'d reach space in about an hour."
"The Moon has no air, so its sky is always black, even in the daytime."
"Earth spins at about 1,600 km/h at the equator — but we don\'t feel it because we spin along with it."
"Compare daylight in the north and south."
"Trace a curve of Earth\'s plate boundaries."
"No recent observations available; the Moon and daylight are still here"
"Sunrise is a moving boundary between darkness and daylight. We\'ll follow it from a marked place."
"Look at London on the globe. Notice which side faces the Sun. The marker and the daylight calculation are separate clues."
"As Earth spins eastward, which way does the dawn boundary move across a map of longitudes?"
"Yes. At a fixed UTC time, the dawn line moves westward over longitudes as Earth rotates east."
"It moves westward across longitudes. Earth itself turns eastward, carrying each place into daylight."
"Move the globe\'s lesson clock forward two hours and watch the light shift. This is a simulation, while Today stays real-time."
"The sunlight direction changed with time. Did the saved place move on the globe?"
"Exactly. The place keeps its coordinates while Earth\'s rotation changes its illumination."
"A place keeps its latitude and longitude. The changing angle to the Sun creates day and night."
"No; Earth rotated relative to the Sun"
"Visit three locations, predict a pattern, then reveal plate boundaries. Historical fallback examples are labelled with dates and sources."
"Historical fallback: 2011-03-11 Tohoku earthquake, USGS. A recent Pacific observation is used when available."
"Historical fallback: 1980-05-18 Mount St. Helens eruption, USGS. This is a dated lesson example, not a live report."
"Historical fallback: 1960-05-22 Great Chilean earthquake, USGS. This example stays outside the live-events repository."
"Which broad pattern links many earthquake and volcano locations around the Pacific?"
"Yes. Many cluster near plate edges, but some events also happen away from mapped boundaries."
"The broad pattern is a belt near several plate edges. Individual events need their own evidence; distance to a line is not a diagnosis."
"One straight line through the Pacific center"
"Every event lies exactly on one boundary"
"Gold lines show a generalized PB2002 plate-boundary model. Compare the Pacific rim; these lines do not explain every individual event."
"Plate motions concentrate many earthquakes and volcanoes around the Pacific. Hotspots and earthquakes within plates show why the pattern has exceptions."
"Compare daylight at London and Sydney on two dates. Earth\'s tilted axis changes how long the Sun stays above the horizon."
"Observe London near the June solstice. The Northern Hemisphere has longer daylight."
"Observe Sydney on the same date. Its winter daylight is shorter than London\'s summer daylight."
"Near the December solstice, which marked place has longer daylight?"
"Yes. The Southern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun in December, so Sydney has longer days."
"Sydney has longer daylight near the December solstice. The Southern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun then."
"Compare the daylight readouts after changing the lesson date. This changes the app scene only."
"Earth\'s axis stays tilted about 23.4° as it orbits the Sun. The Northern and Southern Hemispheres alternate longer daylight. The visible guides mark the equator, tropics, and polar circles."
"A voice for this language is not installed on this device."
"Earth’s axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees relative to its orbit around the Sun."
